summary: Describes how the IETF's separate standards fit together to support emergency calls over the Internet, from citizens and visitors to the authorities. It is informational and ties together location, call routing and signaling pieces. It was later updated by RFC 7852.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 6443 explains how Internet devices can place emergency calls that reach an appropriate call center. It describes how a device gets its location, how a lookup service maps that location to a center, and how the call carries location and callback information. The document is a framework and leaves required device and network behavior to a separate best-current-practice document.

subtitle: How location, call routing, and Internet signaling combine to reach an emergency call center.

tldr.problem: An Internet emergency call depends on many parties and separate protocols to identify the call, determine location, route it, and let responders call back.
tldr.mechanism: The framework marks the call with an emergency service URN, maps location to a PSAP with LoST, and carries location in SIP signaling to the emergency services network.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6443 is an Informational framework, not a specification of normative behavior. It was later updated by RFC 7852.

today: RFC 6443 is Informational and has been updated by RFC 7852. It was not obsoleted; its normative requirements are described in a separate best-current-practice document.

sections.title: Scope and Goals
sections.content:
RFC 6443 describes calls from citizens or visitors to a Public Safety Answering Point (PSAP), a call center that answers emergency calls. It focuses on Internet devices and PSAPs that can handle Internet multimedia calls. Gateways to legacy telephone systems are outside its scope.

The framework uses SIP and existing mechanisms; it does not define new SIP headers, methods, status codes, or message bodies. From the PSAP's perspective, the call should reach the right center based mainly on caller location, provide location precise enough to dispatch help, and allow the PSAP to contact the caller again if the call is disrupted.
sections.plainLanguage: An Internet emergency call must reach the appropriate call center, provide a location that supports dispatch, and include a way to call the person back. RFC 6443 explains how existing protocols can support those goals.

sections.title: How an Emergency Call Is Placed
sections.content:
A device recognizes an emergency dial string and marks the SIP request with a service URN, such as urn:service:sos. The device obtains location from a measurement or from its access network, then queries LoST to map that location and service to a PSAP URI. It can cache earlier results and use them if a fresh lookup fails or takes too long.

The device sends a SIP INVITE with the emergency URN, PSAP URI, and location. Proxies route it to an Emergency Services Routing Proxy (ESRP), which selects a PSAP. The PSAP's response returns to the caller, and an ACK completes call setup.
sections.plainLanguage: The device gets its location and asks LoST which emergency call center serves it. It then sends a SIP call request with the emergency service and location information so proxies can route it to that center.

sections.title: Finding and Conveying Location
sections.content:
Location supports both call routing and responder dispatch. Routing may use a coarse location when a precise fix would take too long; the framework notes that some cold starts can take as much as 30 seconds. A more accurate dispatch location can be sent later. Location may be civic, geospatial, or based on a cell tower and sector.

Devices may get location from a network Location Information Server using DHCP, HELD, or LLDP-MED, or may use a locally measured or manually entered value. The device should send the location in the form in which it was determined. Converting between civic and geospatial forms before delivery can introduce errors if databases differ. If several locations are available, the routing element must choose exactly one for its LoST query.
sections.plainLanguage: A device can learn its location from the network or measure it itself. The call should carry the original location, because converting between address formats can introduce errors.

sections.title: Routing the Call to a PSAP
sections.content:
LoST maps a location and an emergency service identifier to one or more URIs. Normal SIP routing resolves the chosen URI to a next hop. Caller location is the primary routing input, though the service type and the caller's media capabilities can also affect which call center or call taker receives the call.

An endpoint can refresh its location and LoST mapping when an emergency call starts, using cached values if either step fails. A proxy may perform mapping when the endpoint cannot, but it may be unable to determine the caller's location. The RFC says a proxy must not ask an endpoint for location through a mechanism that would expose it to any proxy on the call path.
sections.plainLanguage: LoST uses the caller's location and requested emergency service to identify a suitable call center. SIP proxies then route the call, and an emergency services proxy can make the final choice of PSAP.

sections.title: Call Signaling and Callback
sections.content:
A SIP INVITE can carry the service URN in its Request-URI, the PSAP URI in a Route header, and location in a Geolocation header. It should also include callback identifiers. The Contact header needs a globally routable URI so the PSAP can call back promptly; a longer-term address of record is also provided.

Emergency calls should disable features such as call waiting, transfer, three-way calling, and hold when they could interfere with handling the call. PSAPs should accept voice and real-time text; the framework also describes instant messaging and video media. Automated tests can check routing, signaling, and media without occupying PSAP staff.
sections.plainLanguage: The call includes contact information so the PSAP can reach the caller again. The framework also describes media support and automated tests that check whether the call path works.

sections.title: Security and Location Privacy
sections.content:
Location and identity information in emergency-call signaling are privacy-sensitive. The framework recommends hop-by-hop protection with TLS or IPsec. End-to-end encryption of SIP signaling cannot hide location from the proxies that need it to route the call.

If a secure connection cannot be established, the call should be retried without it. The RFC considers completing an emergency call more important than protecting the data in that case, while acknowledging that an unprotected call can reveal information such as location.
sections.plainLanguage: The framework recommends encrypting call signaling as it travels between network elements. If encryption cannot be set up, it says to try the call without it so a security failure does not prevent a request for help.
